title: Conscience
hookLine: the inner voice, formed by prayer and learning, to be followed

cards: A cave in the wilderness. In the dark at the back, David and his men are hiding from King Saul, who has come with an army to kill him. Then Saul himself walks into the very same cave, alone, with no idea who's in there.
David's men whisper: this is the day. God has handed him to you. David creeps forward in the dark and quietly cuts a corner off the king's robe.
That's all. Then he goes back. And the text says: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt."
Not for killing him. For a piece of cloth.

teach.b: Something in David spoke up, and over something small. His men saw a chance. His conscience saw the king.
David tells his men he will not lift his hand against "the LORD's anointed," and he holds them back. Christians call that inner voice conscience, and Paul writes about it.
He describes people who never had the law of Moses but still know right from wrong, the work of the law "written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness."
A witness inside, sometimes accusing, sometimes excusing. Then a caution: Christian teaching says conscience has to be formed. It isn't automatically right.
It can be dulled by habit, made too harsh, or trained by a crowd. Paul spends whole chapters on believers whose consciences disagree about what's allowed, and asks them to be patient with each other.
So Christians tend a conscience the way you tend a garden: with prayer, scripture, the teaching of their church, and honest friends.
A psalm puts the prayer side simply: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." And once it's formed, conscience is to be followed.
Paul tells a Roman governor, in Acts, that he works "to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men." Churches speak of this in their own ways.
Catholic teaching calls conscience a judgment a person must obey, and must also form.
Some Protestant teachers speak of a conscience bound to scripture. In both, it's the place where a person stands alone before God.

how: Christians form conscience through prayer, scripture, the teaching of their church and the counsel of others, and some examine their conscience at the end of the day or before confession or communion.

o: an inner witness to right and wrong
the guilty feeling you get after being caught
a sense of right and wrong that's never mistaken

games.q: the inner witness — tap the pairs.
p: cut a corner off Saul's robe

s: Christian teaching says conscience is always right as it is
it has to be formed, with prayer, scripture and teaching, and then followed.
David's conscience troubled him for cutting a piece of Saul's robe
"David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt."
Paul says only people who had the law of Moses have a conscience
he says people without that law still have it "written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness."

games.q: you're David, hiding in a cave. the king who is hunting you walks in alone. your men whisper, "this is the day." what do you do?
o: cut a corner off his robe, and then hold your men back.
games.why: David cuts off a corner of the robe, and even that troubles him: his heart smote him. he restrains his men and lets Saul walk out.

practice: Let the last day or two pass slowly through your mind, a conversation, an email, a choice, and see if there's a small place where something tugged, the way David's heart smote him over a corner of cloth.
Don't argue with it yet, and don't punish yourself; just listen. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: search me, O God, and know my heart.

wordCard.voice: Conscience. The inner witness that knows right from wrong, formed by prayer and learning, and then followed.

orig.note: Greek: conscience, an inner knowing. Paul's word in Romans 2:15 and Acts 24:16.

carryVoice: Your line: the inner voice. Formed first, with care, and then followed. See you tomorrow.
